strengths: Identifies and characterizes an interesting and underexplored failure mode (semantic collapsing problem) with careful, multi-faceted empirical analysis, including textual-space distance metrics (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL), embedding norm histograms, and CLIP alignment tracking over training iterations.
The analysis distinguishing SCP from language drift and identifying unconstrained embedding norm/direction drift as the root cause is a useful conceptual contribution.

Proposed fix (SLERP-based test-time embedding adjustment) is simple, training-free, and broadly applicable post hoc to multiple personalization paradigms (Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, Custom Diffusion) without retraining.

Extensive experimental coverage: two datasets (CC101, CelebA-HQ), multiple baselines, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (α, β), and a large appendix with additional qualitative/quantitative results and multi-concept experiments.
Interesting finding of the 'two-way' (positive and negative) impact of SCP on generation quality, adding nuance to the problem framing.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains from the proposed method are generally small (CLIP-T full-prompt improvements of ~0.3-1.9 points) and frequently accompanied by non-trivial drops in visual fidelity metrics (CLIP-I/DINO-I), e.g., -4.55 for DB+TEA on CelebA and -3.81 DINO-I for TI+TEA on CC101, making the net benefit of the method unclear without a more holistic trade-off metric or Pareto analysis.

No human/user study is conducted despite the central claims being about perceptual quality and semantic richness of generated images; reliance solely on CLIP/DINO scores is a known limitation for such alignment claims.

The method's positive effects seem sensitive to prompt type and concept, and the paper's own analysis (Section 3.2.2/3.3) shows SCP is sometimes beneficial for generation quality, yet the proposed fix does not adaptively distinguish between cases where reversing drift helps vs. hurts—undermining the motivation given the paper's own two-way-impact finding.
Fixed, globally-set hyperparameters (α=0.2, β=1.5) are chosen heuristically rather than through a principled or prompt-adaptive procedure, which the authors themselves flag as a limitation.

Missing comparisons against alternative existing regularization-based mitigations (e.g., prior-preservation loss variants, weight regularization methods cited in the related work) as baselines for reducing prompt misalignment; the paper only compares each baseline against its own +TEA variant.

The core technical contribution (SLERP interpolation toward the original word embedding with a scale factor) is relatively simple and somewhat expected once the diagnosis (norm/direction drift) is established; the main novelty lies in the diagnostic analysis rather than the fix itself.
Only evaluated on Stable Diffusion v1.5; generalization to more modern/large-scale T2I backbones (SDXL, SD2, diffusion transformers) is untested, limiting claims of broad applicability.

Some redundant/duplicated text (e.g., repeated paragraph in Section 2) suggests limited polish, and the write-up of qualitative 'improvement' claims (e.g., 'cool effects') is somewhat informal for a rigorous evaluation.

strengths: The paper identifies and names an interesting failure mode (Semantic Collapsing Problem) that is distinct from the well-studied 'language drift' problem, and provides a reasonably thorough empirical investigation of it in both textual embedding space and generated image space.

The empirical analysis uses multiple complementary distance metrics (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL) and alignment scores (CLIP-T/I, DINO) to triangulate evidence for the phenomenon, which is a nice methodological effort.

The proposed fix (SLERP-based magnitude/direction realignment) is simple, training-free, and architecture-agnostic, and the authors demonstrate it can be applied post-hoc to three different personalization paradigms (TI, DreamBooth, Custom Diffusion).

The paper includes an interesting multi-concept extension analysis showing SCP can also occur/intensify between two personalized tokens competing for dominance, which is a useful observation for future work.
Extensive appendix with qualitative examples, dataset descriptions, and additional plots supporting reproducibility of the analysis.
weaknesses: The quantitative improvements from the proposed TEA method are very small and inconsistent: average CLIP-f_T gains are only 0.09–1.9 points, frequently accompanied by non-trivial drops in CLIP-I/DINO-I (e.g., -2.34 to -4.55), so it is unclear the method yields a net practical benefit rather than simply trading one metric for another via the same magnitude/direction knobs.

No comparison to any existing baselines or prior techniques that address related issues (e.g., prior-preservation regularization, weight-space regularization methods like SVDiff/OFT, or other multi-concept composition methods like Break-a-Scene, Custom Diffusion's own regularization, MultiBooth). Without such comparisons it is impossible to assess whether TEA is actually better than simpler/known fixes, undermining the significance claim.

The core method is effectively a straightforward SLERP interpolation toward the base concept embedding — a well-known operation — applied in a fairly direct way; the technical novelty is limited once the SCP diagnosis itself is set aside.

Hyperparameters (α, β) are fixed globally and chosen heuristically; the paper itself acknowledges in Limitations that fixed hyperparameters are suboptimal across prompts, yet no adaptive or principled selection strategy is proposed or evaluated, weakening the practical utility of the method.

The two-way (positive and negative) impact of SCP described in Section 3.2.2 undermines the motivation for a single fixed corrective procedure: the method cannot distinguish when SCP is beneficial (subject must be dominant to be recognizable) versus harmful, yet it is applied uniformly, so it may hurt cases where SCP was actually helping.

Evaluation relies solely on automated CLIP/DINO alignment metrics without any human perceptual study, despite qualitative claims such as 'more coherent and realistic images' — these claims are not rigorously substantiated.

Evaluation scale is limited: 9 CC101 concepts and 10 CelebA identities with a single base model (SD v1.5), and results have high variance (large standard deviations in Table 1), raising concerns about statistical significance of the reported gains.
The manuscript has editorial issues, including a verbatim repeated paragraph in Section 2 (duplicate text about the keyword V*), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

The 'root cause' claim (unconstrained optimization causes drift) is demonstrated empirically via norm/cosine-similarity tracking but not formally analyzed or theoretically justified; alternative explanations (e.g., simply the model learning a highly discriminative/rare token due to limited images) are not ruled out via ablation.

strengths: Identifies and names a specific, under-explored failure mode (semantic collapsing problem) with a reasonably thorough empirical characterization, including textual-space distance analyses (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL) and image-space alignment score tracking over training iterations.

Proposes a simple, lightweight, training-free test-time embedding adjustment (SLERP-based rotation + magnitude rescaling) that can be applied post-hoc to multiple personalization methods (TI, DreamBooth, Custom Diffusion) without retraining or architecture changes.

Broad empirical coverage across two datasets (CustomConcept101, CelebA-HQ) and three baseline personalization methods, plus an interesting extension to multi-concept personalization showing concept dominance dynamics.
Extensive appendix with additional qualitative examples, ablations on hyperparameters α and β, and detailed experimental protocol description aiding reproducibility.
The two-way (positive and negative) impact analysis of SCP is a nuanced and somewhat novel observation that adds depth beyond a simple 'collapse is always bad' narrative.
weaknesses: Quantitative improvements from TEA are small and inconsistent: CLIPf_T gains range from only 0.09 to 1.9 across settings, and CLIP-I/DINO scores frequently decrease (sometimes substantially, e.g., -4.55 for DB+TEA on CelebA), indicating a real trade-off rather than a clear win, which is not strongly emphasized in the main text framing.

No comparison against existing mitigation techniques for language drift/overfitting mentioned in the related work (e.g., prior-preservation loss variants, orthogonal fine-tuning, weight regularization methods like SVDiff); the paper only compares baselines vs. baselines+TEA, leaving it unclear whether TEA is better than, complementary to, or redundant with established regularization approaches.

Evaluation relies exclusively on CLIP/DINO embedding-based metrics, which are known to be limited in capturing fine-grained compositional alignment; no human evaluation or user study is provided despite the paper's central claim being about perceptual/semantic composition quality.

Fixed hyperparameters (α=0.2, β=1.5) are used globally despite the paper's own analysis showing substantial prompt-dependent sensitivity and the 'two-way impact' finding that SCP can sometimes be beneficial — this undercuts the practical robustness of a single fixed adjustment and is acknowledged only as future work rather than addressed.

The identified 'root cause' (unconstrained optimization leading to embedding norm/direction drift) is a fairly expected and intuitive finding rather than a deeply surprising mechanistic insight, and gradient clipping/weight decay baselines are discussed but not empirically compared against.
Limited model scope: only Stable Diffusion v1.5 is tested; no validation on more modern/larger T2I backbones (SDXL, etc.), limiting claims of general applicability.

The DreamBooth-specific prompt-level adjustment (Eq. 2) is a somewhat ad hoc workaround necessitated by the method not maintaining an explicit token embedding, raising questions about principled generality of the approach across architectures.

Statistical rigor is inconsistent — most result tables (6, 7) lack error bars/variance, making it hard to assess whether the modest gains are statistically meaningful given the small benchmark sizes (9-10 concepts, limited prompts).

strengths: The paper identifies and carefully characterizes an interesting phenomenon, the 'Semantic Collapsing Problem' (SCP), distinguishing it from the well-known 'language drift' issue, and supports it with a fairly thorough empirical analysis using multiple distance metrics (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL divergence) in both textual embedding space and image space.

The proposed Test-time Embedding Adjustment (TEA) is simple, training-free, and lightweight, requiring no modification to model weights, which makes it easy to plug into many existing personalization pipelines.

Breadth of empirical validation is commendable: the method is tested across multiple personalization frameworks (Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, Custom Diffusion, ClassDiffusion, EasyControl, ReVersion), two architectures (Stable Diffusion and Flux), and several datasets (CustomConcept101, CelebA-HQ, Relationship), with extensive qualitative examples in the appendix.

The discovery that TEA can partially reverse the protective effect of Anti-DreamBooth is a novel and interesting finding, raising legitimate questions about the robustness/false sense of security offered by current anti-personalization/adversarial defense mechanisms.
The appendix is extensive, offering hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (alpha, beta), multi-concept SCP analysis, and reasonably detailed experimental/reproducibility setup.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains from TEA are often small and inconsistent: many CLIP-I/DINO-I scores decrease (e.g., -2.37 for DB+TEA and -3.81 for TI+TEA on CelebA in Table 1), and the paper does not provide a clear, principled Pareto-style analysis of the fidelity/context alignment trade-off, making it hard to assess practical significance of the improvements.

No human/user study is conducted to validate whether the reported CLIP/DINO metric changes correspond to perceptually meaningful improvements in image quality or prompt alignment; reliance solely on automated metrics is a notable limitation given known weaknesses of CLIP-based scores for fine-grained personalization evaluation.

The paper does not compare against the most directly relevant training-time regularization baseline, PALP (Arar et al., 2024), which explicitly regularizes the learned token toward its class concept—conceptually very similar to what TEA does at test time. Without this comparison, it is hard to judge whether TEA offers a genuine advantage over existing regularization-based solutions besides being 'training-free'.

Hyperparameters (alpha for rotation, beta for scaling) are fixed globally across all prompts/methods, and the paper itself acknowledges in the Limitations section that fixed hyperparameters may not be optimal for all prompts, with no principled or adaptive method proposed for their selection.

The method's simplicity (uniform adjustment across all embedding dimensions) is acknowledged as a limitation, and its extension to non-CLIP text encoders (e.g., T5 used in Flux-based EasyControl) is not clearly justified theoretically, raising questions about generality beyond CLIP-style single-token embeddings.

Error bars/variance and number of seeds are inconsistently reported; while some analyses average over 50-100 random runs, the main results tables (Tables 1, 2, 6, 7) report single-point estimates without variance, making it difficult to assess statistical robustness of the reported improvements.

The manuscript has apparent preparation issues, e.g., abstract and conclusion end with truncated sentences ('Our code is published a', 'More results ... can be found a'), suggesting incomplete removal of anonymized links/careless editing, which detracts from polish expected at a top venue.

The 'surprising vulnerability' finding on Anti-DreamBooth is only demonstrated for a single anti-personalization method; no broader anti-personalization/adversarial protection techniques (e.g., Glaze, Mist, PhotoGuard) are tested, limiting the generality of the claimed security implications.
